comments.raw_comment:
The graph shows the average egg price over time generally increased, but the price fluctuated greatly in many years.  The most noticeable price fluctuations occurred around 2004, 2008, 2015, and 2022.  The first price spike occurred in 2004 but returned to a lower price quickly.  Around 2008, the egg price spiked, but increased and decreased more gradually than the other years.  The 2008 spike was the first time egg price exceeded $3.  In 2015, the average price of a dozen eggs increased by about $1 then dropped by about $1.50.  The most recent recorded increase shows a steep increase by nearly $2.50 in one year.  Because the writers adjusted for inflation, I wonder what major events relate to the price spikes, and if we can categorize the events.  For example, do the price spikes relate to political strife such as a war, or was there a disease plaguing major egg production areas, so people harvested fewer eggs?   I do not eat eggs frequently, so I did not notice the increased egg prices, but the article highlights that an American person “consumed an average of 278 eggs last year,” so Americans must allocate more funds to groceries, or consume fewer eggs (Network).  Allocating more funds to groceries implies that people either work more hours at jobs, or depreciate other areas in their life such as entertainment and utilities.  Consuming fewer eggs suggests people change their diets and find egg alternatives.  

Egg-streme Price Spikes: Don’t Put Eggs in Your Basket

comments.raw_comment:
I have noticed that in the recent years, the prices of eggs have skyrocketed, being more expensive than ever before. Since 2000, egg prices seemed to fluctuate with a gradual increase. However, the past few years after 2020 have seen significantly less fluctuation than the other years and rather a steep increase in egg prices per dozen. 

I wonder what the economical and environmental effects that may have caused this sudden increase are. The rapid spike in egg prices leads me to think that some environmental factor may be causing chickens to die at higher rates than ever before, leading to an egg shortage, higher demand, and therefore increased prices.  

This directly relates to my family and I, as we are avid consumers of eggs. We like eating them plain for breakfast, as well as putting them in dishes. Needless to say, we consume many eggs throughout the week and frequently have to buy more. This sudden increase in prices has impacted us, as we are more mindful of how much we spend on eggs and how rapidly we consume them. With the prices of eggs becoming more expensive, lower income individuals are less likely to be able to afford them in more recent years than they were before. This eliminates a healthy option available to them for meals, making them more likely to turn to less healthy alternatives that are high in sugars and fats.  

Egg Prices on the Rise – But for Good This Time

comments.raw_comment:
In this graph, I notice that from the year 2000 to December 2022, the monthly average price of a dozen eggs has gradually increased from around $1.50 to nearly $4.25. Besides this gradual increase, I also notice a stark decrease in average price in 2016 from about $3.30 to $1.80, almost reducing the price in half. This has me wonder whether there was a certain policy that was put into action in 2016 that caused the decline of eggs. This could be concluded with inflation, but unlikely. I also notice a skyrocketing price of eggs in 2022. This also has me wondering whether there are some lasting effects from COVID-19 that have caused the surge in price.

As someone that regularly eats eggs for breakfast, this definitely has an effect on my daily routine, as I have been warier about purchasing eggs recently and have sought alternative breakfast choices. Furthermore, eggs are an American staple, meaning that this surge in price has likely had similar effects on many people across the United States. This could potentially mean that there is some distress in the agricultural sectors too, where chickens might not be laying enough eggs satisfactory enough for consumption. This could lead to a decrease in supply with the same amount of demand, and basic economic principles tell us that the price should increase.

I think a catchy title for this may be “Consumers are Scrambling for Cheap Eggs”

What do you wonder?

How does this relate to me and my community?

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that since 2000, the prices for a dozen eggs have fluctuated and gone from as high as over $3.50 to around $1.75 in a year or two. Ever since it hit that low in 2016/2017 the prices had stayed relatively the same until the recent spike after 2020 and the most recent price on the graph being $4.25. I also noted that egg prices are the highest they’ve been in over 20 years.

What do you wonder?
I wonder if the prices recently spiked as a result of the war between Russia and Ukraine and the U.S losing a valuable supply chain. I also wonder what caused the significant decrease in the price of eggs after 2015 since no graphs were provided for what may have happened to decrease egg prices by such a significant amount.

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community and I because eggs are a staple in most households including mine. With eggs being at a higher price and seemingly getting higher it may become harder to buy as many eggs as normal, many people may also stop buying and eating eggs altogether. There are also many households that have likely depended on eggs being a low price because they’re a good source of protein and sometimes they may not have enough money to buy things such as chicken or steak.

1. The average price of a dozen eggs reached its greatest point in December 2022, when it was $4.25, while it appeared to have been at its lowest point around the estimate of the year 2019. The underlying factors that appear to suit the data displayed in the graph are that the prices are so high due to the high cost of the grains used to feed the birds, as well as the additional factor that there is less egg-laying occurring. Raising the price of eggs would be the only way to solve this if there weren't actually any eggs being sold because fewer eggs were being laid by birds and the cost of feeding them was expensive.
2. I'm curious as to why this might be as to what factors generally induce inflation in eggs. Do global effects have an effect on what is going on with the inflation of eggs? Since egg prices generally seemed to be rising years ago, I ponder what it would take to bring them down. When will the cost become too high to bear? Have we hit the peak, or will it keep rising?
3. This relates to me and my community because in my house, one of the most consumed resources in my house. Also, since it is one of the most consumed things, it sometimes turns into a supply and demand since so many people want to accumulate it because it may go out of stock. 1. Over the past 20 years, the cost of eggs has increased to an all-time high. Around 2016, a second, smaller peak occurred. Have hens formed a union and are they refusing to put in the long, arduous hours they once did? Eggs are the poster child for this trend because they are a staple on grocery shop lists and are now known for not being prohibitively costly. I can only infer that grocery stores and food in general are becoming more expensive.

3. I think that most societies and populations depend on food. Most families visit the grocery store once a week, and I would imagine that the majority of them purchase eggs. My family has reportedly grumbled about the cost of eggs. I therefore cannot presume that other families in my neighborhood are also upset about the increase in egg pricing.

4. "Rise of the Planet of the Eggs"

What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?
Around 2021 to the present, I noticed a sharp increase in egg prices. Even when the price was increased in 2015, when it was about $3.75, I've noticed that it's now at its highest point ever at $4.25. I've noticed that there hasn't been a time when prices have remained constant over the past twenty years. Either they are gradually rising or falling.  Which demonstrates how severe inflation has become and how gradually fewer eggs are being laid by chickens today than they were a few years ago. 

What do you wonder?
I'm curious as to why the price went up in the first place. Does this mean that the chickens that we lost to avian flu aren't laying as many eggs, or that there is inflammation? A further question I have is whether the price will go down again or if it will only go up from here. 

How does this relate to you and your community?
Due to the fact that I come from a small town where the majority of the population is from the lower to middle class, the increased cost of goods like eggs has an impact on both my community and me. These people must forgo some things because they cannot afford to buy them for their families, who they must support and feed.

What do you notice?
In this graph, the most noticeable thing has to be the extensive plummet of the line and how high it rises right after 2021. The price of eggs has always differed throughout the years ranging from around $1.75 in the 2000s to $2-3 in 2010. That is why the huge increase in the price of eggs in 2021 which costs almost twice as much as the average stands out. I also notice the cost to feed chicken has gone up, as the cost of barley and corn has duplicated. Not only this but March of 2022 was the highest month for chickens dying from the Avian flu.
What do you wonder?
I understand why the price of eggs has increased, there is no way to change the price of food to feed chickens or bring back the chickens lost to the Avian flu. What I wonder is when the prices of eggs will drop once again. Inflation has been going on for about a year or two now, but when are the prices gonna follow a pattern and drop once again?
How does this impact me and my community?
This impacts my community and me because it is very concerning to be on top of the prices of everything rising something as simple as eggs are now twice their original price. In a small town like the one I live in, something so small can largely impact my community and the amount of money they have left to provide for their families.

comments.raw_comment:
1) I noticed that the jump from eggs being a dollar in 2020-2021 quickly skyrocketed to 4.25 by 2022. It was a dramatic jump indicating a change within the economy otherwise known as inflation. As much as I knew egg prices were rising in our country, a visual graph gave me a clear view of why several are complaining about this sudden change. I never knew eggs were $1 at one point. The graph fluctuates with four high peaks at most. Evidence of the rising egg prices is supported by the growing price rate of 2021-2022.

2) I wonder, as dumb as this question may be, is the economy the problem here, or is the number of farms that are providing the eggs going out of business? Are there any connections between the rising of egg prices to the rising of gas prices as well?

3) This relates to my community because going to the grocery now has become a financial challenge due to the fact that pretty much everything has increased in its price. Now that I'm reaching adulthood, this inflation of products opened my eyes to how financially smart I have to be in what I purchase. College alone is expensive, now my sunny-side-ups are leaning towards the same path. 

4) Why are the prices of eggs increasing? EGGFLATION is the answer.

comments.raw_comment:
1) Egg prices in the United States peaked in this year. Previously, the highest average price was in 2015, when a dozen eggs cost 2.75 U.S. dollars on average. The price of eggs has been gradually increasing over the last twenty years, and that there has been a spike in egg prices in the last three years, around the same time that inflation has increased quickly and the price of products has skyrocketed. Furthermore, in the third image [Egg-Laying Birds Lost To Avian Flu In 2022], we get some background for the current increase in egg prices. Not only is inflation out of control, but the number of egg-laying birds is declining, resulting in a higher demand for eggs and a lower supply, culminating in a price increase.

2) I wonder if, similar to how egg prices fell after the Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) outbreak that affected US poultry farms between December 2014 and June 2015, egg prices will fall after the 2023 avian flu. I wonder how this inflation of eggs will affect other aspects of the food industry that use eggs within their dishes.

3) This is relevant to my community because eggs are a common staple in most homes and used to be a cheaper choice for a simple meal or for protein in diets; now, they are tougher to come by, and families across the country will have to either pay the additional money or give up eggs. 

4) Cracking the Case on the Egg-cessive Inflation of Eggs

1) I notice that in the Monthly average price of a dozen eggs, the graph shows that the price of eggs increases on a cycle, increasing and decreasing as time goes on. There are a couple of peak times when egg prices reach a high before coming down again. This is shown in 2004 when egg prices are at a high, then in 2005 when they hit a low. This is shown again in 2015 when the prices hit a high and in 2016 when the prices hit a low.

2) I wonder if the Annual prices of grains used for feed continue to increase if the prices of eggs will grow even more in 5 years than what they are now.

3) This is relevant to my community and me because many people in Portsmouth eat eggs, and my family also eats eggs. In Newington and Portsmouth, a lot of people have chickens in their backyards, eating the eggs from their chickens. If egg prices continue to increase, more people will probably choose to own chickens. Eggs are a necessary ingredient in a lot of different foods and are needed in a staple diet.

4) A dozen eggs are soon to be a dozen dollars?!

comments.raw_comment:
* The first graph [Monthly Average Price Of A Dozen Eggs] indicates a strong, positive relationship between the price of eggs and the month/year in which the data was collected. This shows that the price of eggs has been steadily increasing over the past twenty years; more specifically, in the past three years, we can see a spike in egg prices around the same time that inflation increased rapidly and the price of goods skyrocketed. Additionally, in the third graph [Egg-Laying Birds Lost To Avian Flu In 2022], we receive some extra context for the spike in egg cost in recent years. Not only is inflation going crazy, but the population of egg-laying birds is also decreasing, resulting in a greater demand for eggs and a lower supply - leading to a price spike.
* I wonder if, as the population of egg-laying birds begins to increase, egg prices will decrease again - or will inflation keep egg prices where they currently are despite the egg-laying birds' population rebound?
* This relates to my community because eggs are a common staple in most households, and used to be a cheaper option for an easy breakfast; now, they are harder to get, and families all over will have to either cough up the extra mula, or give up their egg-loving lifestyles. One of my friends has a bunch of happy "egg-laying birds," so I personally am not deeply affected by this unfortunate price spike.
* Big Eggs-pectations For Future "Egg-Laying Bird" Populations

1) I notice that the price of feeding grains is at the highest it has been in almost a decade, and according to the right graph, there was an outbreak of avian flu in March and April that led to the loss of a combined 25 million hens. 2) I wonder if the loss of hens and the growing price of grains has actually harmed farming corporations. The most recent articles I've seen on the topic has claimed that these companies have been recording record profits in their egg sales, which seems to be the opposite of what is expected after such a large hit to egg production. Are the grain prices and avian flu really the cause of high egg prices? Or is there a lurking variable underneath it all?

3) Grocery prices are one of the places where low-income communities get hit hardest by inflation. When every dollar counts in a weekly grocery trip, the insane price of eggs is something that really weighs in your pockets after only a couple months. Personally, people in my community have been helping out where it's needed by sharing cartons of eggs in their workplaces, and my neighbors have traded eggs with us for fish and other meats. While the situation might not be ideal, it helps highlight the way that communities lend help in times of need.

1. I've noticed that egg prices will hit an all-time high in December 2022. The path to $4.25 has risen and fallen steadily over the years, with the most notable peaks occurring in 2008, 2016, and 2022. The lowest peaks occurred in the 2000s and near the beginning of COVID in 2019. Looking at the extra graph "Annual prices of grains used for feed," it does appear that the grain price had a significant impact on the price of eggs around the year 2012 as the prices had reached their peak.
2. Is the sharp rise in egg prices due to the loss of more than 15 million egg-laying birds due to avian flu in 2022? Also, why were egg prices significantly lower in the years leading up to the pandemic and for the first two years following it?
3. This is significant in my community because the majority of us have had to deal with the financial consequences of COVID, and as the price of eggs rises, so does the price of everything else. Simple foods like eggs have become more expensive for people in financial difficulty. There is more of a supply problem than a demand problem, though both are present. Egg prices are affected by the chickens that lay the eggs, which are currently more expensive to feed. With all these factors that contribute to the supply of eggs, being able to provide food for families is more difficult and more of a strain than ever.
4. What is Up with the Eggflation: Prices are More Scrambled than Ever!

1. I noticed that every couple of years, there seems to be a pattern since at a certain point the prices drastically increase, they slowly decrease and stay constant for a while until it happens again. Also, after 2015 was the first time eggs went back down to the 1 dollar range since almost 2007. I noticed the increase in price that is happening after 2020 has the steepest slope. The price of eggs before it started increasing was lower than the price of eggs at the start of the graph in 2000.
2. I wonder if all the increases in the prices of eggs were due to recessions during those years. I wonder why after 2015, the price decreased by a large amount unlike the other times when the price was high but would be lowered by smaller amounts. I also wonder about the max price for eggs until people stop buying them and how the current price has affected the number of eggs sold.
3. This relates to me and my community because back then my family would buy two cartons of 24 eggs and after the price has increased a lot, we only buy one carton. Also, I have noticed that after the price has changed, my family has used less eggs and are finding alternatives to eat with their meals. Coming from an area that has a lot of minorities the price change has affected what people eat because eggs can be part of a meal for many that don't have much so now the cost affects what people are eating.
4. The Scramble of Egg Prices Over The Years

comments.raw_comment:
1.  I've noticed that the price of eggs reaches an all-time high in December 2022. The path to $4.25 has been steadily increasing and decreasing over the years, with the most notable peaks occurring in 2008, 2016, and 2022. The lowest peaks occurred in the 2000s and around 2019, near the start of COVID. Looking at the extra graph "Annual prices of grains used for feed" around the year 2012, when the grain price was at its highest, it does not appear to have had a significant impact on the price of eggs.

2.  I'm curious how the prices of feed grains correlate with the prices of eggs. Is the dramatic rise in egg prices due to the loss of more than 15 million egg-laying birds to avian flu in 2022? Also, why were egg prices much lower in the years preceding the pandemic and for the first two years following the pandemic?

3. This is relevant to my community because the majority of us have had to deal with the financial consequences of COVID, and as the price of eggs rises, so does the price of everything else in the market. It has become more difficult for people who are struggling financially to afford simple foods like eggs.

4. "Laying Egg Prices In Recent Years"
